title: Wills and Trusts
description: Comprehensive will and trust planning to protect your assets and provide for your loved ones according to your wishes.

overview.heading: Practice area
overview.description: Wills and trusts are fundamental estate planning documents that ensure your assets are distributed according to your wishes. A will provides clear instructions for asset distribution after your death, while trusts offer additional benefits including probate avoidance, privacy, and more control over how and when assets are distributed to beneficiaries.

faq.heading: Wills and trusts
faq.description: Common questions about wills and trusts:

items.question: What's the difference between a will and a trust?
items.answer: A will is a legal document that directs how your assets will be distributed after your death and goes through probate court. A trust is a legal arrangement where a trustee holds and manages assets for beneficiaries, can avoid probate, and may offer tax benefits and more control over distribution timing.

items.question: Do I need both a will and a trust?
items.answer: Many people benefit from having both. Even with a trust, you typically need a 'pour-over' will to catch any assets not transferred to the trust. The combination provides comprehensive coverage and ensures all assets are properly handled according to your wishes.

items.question: Can I change my will or trust after I create it?
items.answer: Yes. A will can be updated at any time by creating a new will or adding a codicil. A revocable living trust can be modified or revoked entirely during your lifetime. We recommend reviewing your documents every 3-5 years or after major life changes.

items.question: What happens to my assets if I don't have a will?
items.answer: If you die without a will (intestate), state law determines how your assets are distributed. This may not match your wishes and can create additional expense and delay for your family. Assets typically go to your closest relatives in a predetermined order set by state statute.
